title: How Government Works
description: What a state is, why people obey one, and how governments are built, compared across the UK, the US, Australia, Germany, India and non-democracies. Each lesson practises one skill on real material: classifying a regime, reading a constitution, computing seats from votes, weighing a philosopher's argument, judging what a court can do, and reading regime and turnout data.
audience: A curious adult who follows the news and wants to understand how governments differ and why. They know that some countries have presidents and others prime ministers, but have not read Hobbes or Madison, a constitution, or a table of seats and votes. No earlier course is needed.
outcomes: You'll be able to say what a described state's claim to obedience rests on (security, consent, custom, a leader, lawful procedure), and apply Locke's test of broken trust to a described government.
You'll be able to classify a described regime by who rules and whose good it serves, and by the four categories of the Regimes of the World data.
You'll be able to read a regime, turnout or population table with its definition in hand, and say what it can and cannot show.
You'll be able to tell from a constitution's text which body holds a power and what checks it, in the United States text of 1787 and the Australian text of 1900.
You'll be able to classify a system as parliamentary, presidential or semi-presidential from how its head of government is chosen and removed.
You'll be able to say what a court can and cannot do about a statute in three different systems.

You'll be able to work out how many seats each party wins from district results, under D'Hondt and under largest remainder with the Hare quota, find a Droop quota, and measure how far seats depart from votes with the Gallagher index.
You'll be able to apply Madison's argument on faction, Mill's principle on liberty and Tocqueville's on the majority to a described case.
You'll be able to tell a federal from a unitary state, and to say whether a referendum passes under a double-majority rule.
You'll be able to judge whether a Security Council resolution would pass, and say why the United Nations is not a world government.

lessons.title: Why obey a state?
lessons.objective: Say, for a described state, what its claim to obedience rests on (security, consent, custom, a leader's qualities or lawful procedure), apply Locke's test of broken trust to a described government, and use the pack's legitimacy scholars to say why obedience holds or fails in real states.

concepts.title: State
concepts.summary: Weber's definition: a compulsory political organisation whose centralised government successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of force within a territory.

concepts.title: Failed state
concepts.summary: A state whose claimed sovereignty over its territory has collapsed or never worked.

concepts.title: Legitimacy
concepts.summary: The right of an authority to rule, as accepted by those it rules.

concepts.title: Foundational and contingent legitimacy
concepts.summary: Mittiga's two parts: ability to ensure safety and security, and exercising power in acceptable ways.

concepts.title: Consent and trust
concepts.summary: Locke: nobody comes under political power without consent, and the people lend power to a government to be used for the ends for which it was lent.

concepts.title: Traditional, charismatic and rational-legal legitimacy
concepts.summary: Weber's three bases of a claim to rule: custom, a leader's personal qualities, and lawful procedure.

misconceptions: Treating state, government and nation as one thing. The pack separates a state (sovereignty over a territory) from a nation (identity and culture) and from a government (people who act as the state's agent) (1M, 1O).

Thinking obedience rests on one thing only, force or consent. The pack's scholars give several bases at once: security (Hobbes, foundational legitimacy), consent and acceptable use of power (Locke, contingent legitimacy), and Weber's custom, personal qualities and lawful procedure (1X, 1AA, 1R to 1T).

Equating legitimacy with popularity or with democracy. Weber held that democracy is unnecessary for legitimacy (1U); Wikipedia says unpopular regimes survive when a small, influential elite considers them legitimate (1V); the Mandate of Heaven is a non-democratic basis (1W).

Taking consent to mean a vote someone actually cast. Wikipedia says Locke meant explicit and implicit consent (1K), and records Hume's objection that consent was never given and cannot be withdrawn by leaving (1J).

Treating legitimacy as abstract. Wikipedia says what builds it is specific to the country (water in Nepal, health in Pakistan) and that armed groups may build it more successfully than the state among some people (1Z).
sequence: A state in the political-science sense: Weber's definition (1L), state against nation (1M), against government (1O), and the Montevideo list (1N). The learner says which of state, government and nation is meant in a described case.
When no one holds the monopoly: the failed state (1P), and Mittiga's foundational legitimacy: a government that cannot provide basic security is not legitimate, if it is even a government (1X, 1Y).

Hobbes's security answer in its political form: covenants without the sword are only words (1A), the commonwealth as one person whose acts all authorise (1B), and why agreement without a power would make a state unnecessary (1C).

Locke's answer: consent (1D), power to carry out a sentence, set beside Hobbes's sword (1E); the test of broken trust (1F), altered elections (1G), a packed assembly (1H) and who judges (1I); Hume's objection (1J) and Wikipedia's account of Locke's consent (1K).

Frames that join the two: Hobbes on security and Locke on liberty (1AA), foundational against contingent legitimacy (1X), instrumental against substantive (1AC); and the plain definition of legitimacy (1Q).
Weber's three types (1R, 1S, 1T), his view that legitimacy need not rest on popular suffrage (1U) and the Mandate of Heaven (1W). The learner sorts six invented claims to rule.

Real states: perceived legitimacy and services (1Z), regimes that survive on an elite's belief (1V), Dahl's reservoir (1AB). Close on the UDHR's Article 21, which puts the will of the people at the base of government's authority (paraphrase only, 11V).
examples: Armed groups hold most of a country's provinces, each running its own courts and tax posts, and the capital's government cannot stop them. Under 1L it has lost the monopoly of legitimate force; under 1Y it fails the test of foundational legitimacy.

A legislature votes to take the farms of everyone in one province and give them to its own members. Under Locke's test (1F) it has put itself in a state of war with the people, who are absolved from further obedience.

Invented claims to rule, one per Weber type: a dynasty in power for six hundred years (traditional); a movement obeying a founder whose personal gifts they trust above any office (charismatic); officials acting under a written code that citizens believe was lawfully made (rational-legal).
Services and legitimacy: in Nepal public water provision was most associated with state legitimacy, in Pakistan health services (1Z).

Overlap: Philosophy: Knowledge, Mind and Ethics has a lesson `the-social-contract` (Hobbes, Locke, Rawls). It teaches Hobbes's state of nature (the weakest can kill the strongest, competition, fear and pride, no farming or trade), the social contract and the sovereign, Locke's law of nature, the person who is judge in their own case, consent and the right to replace a government, then Rawls's veil of ignorance with maximin and the difference principle, and has a pair question on what Hobbes and Locke disagree about before there is any government. This lesson leaves those alone and treats the two as answers to a political question about real states: what makes obedience hold. See plan-notes.

lessons.title: Classifying a regime
lessons.objective: Classify a described regime by who rules and whose good the rule serves (Aristotle), and by the four categories of the Regimes of the World classification, and say why a description that fits no box is still informative.

concepts.title: Aristotle's six forms
concepts.summary: Rule by one, few or many, for the common good (kingdom, aristocracy, and what Jowett calls a state) or for the rulers' own good (tyranny, oligarchy, democracy).

concepts.title: Closed autocracy
concepts.summary: A regime in which citizens cannot choose the chief executive or the legislature through multi-party elections.

concepts.title: Electoral autocracy
concepts.summary: A regime with multi-party elections that lacks the freedoms, such as association and expression, that make them meaningful, free and fair.

concepts.title: Electoral democracy
concepts.summary: A regime with meaningful, free and fair multi-party elections.

concepts.title: Liberal democracy
concepts.summary: An electoral democracy that also protects individual and minority rights, equality before the law, and constrains the executive through the legislature and courts.

concepts.title: Hybrid regime
concepts.summary: A regime combining democratic and autocratic features.

misconceptions: Reading Aristotle's 'democracy' as the modern word. For him it is the corrupt form: the poor ruling in their own interest (2C). His good form of rule by the many is 'a state' in Jowett's translation (2B).
Thinking number separates oligarchy from democracy. Aristotle says wealth does: where the rich rule, few or many, it is an oligarchy (2D).

Treating a regime that holds elections as a democracy. Electoral autocracies hold multi-party elections but lack freedoms that make them meaningful (2L), and authoritarian states can hold managed elections (2G).
Sorting every regime into one of two boxes. Wikipedia says democracy and authoritarianism can be thought of as poles on a scale (2H), and hybrid regimes mix them (2I).
sequence: Start with two questions Aristotle puts to any constitution (2A): how many hold the supreme power, and whose good does it serve. The learner names six invented rules.
Give his six names (2B, 2C) and correct the misreading of 'democracy'; add his refinement on wealth (2D) and his test (2E).
Move to the modern words: narrow and broad definitions of democracy (2F) and liberal democracy as a limit on the majority (2P).
Authoritarian features, managed elections and the scale from democratic to authoritarian (2G, 2H).

The four categories in the data (2K to 2N) as three questions in order: can citizens choose by multi-party elections, are the elections meaningful and free, do rights and constraints on the executive exist. The learner sorts invented descriptions.
Hybrid regimes and the gray zone (2I, 2J): a description that fits between boxes, and how to say so.
Parties in autocracies and democracies (2Q): a single governing party does not by itself decide the category.
examples: Invented descriptions, labelled as such: ten wealthy families keep the offices and spend the treasury on their estates (oligarchy in Aristotle's sense); multi-party elections are held, but the opposition's newspapers are closed in each campaign (electoral autocracy); elections are free and fair but the courts do not check the president (electoral democracy).
Aristotle's cases: one person rules for the benefit of all citizens (kingdom); the many, mostly poor, rule in their own interest (democracy in his sense); the many rule for the common good (a state).

lessons.title: Reading regime and turnout data
lessons.objective: Read a regime series, a population count and a turnout series with their definitions in hand, compute a share from counts, and say what a number can and cannot show.

concepts.title: Coded series
concepts.summary: A series in which experts assign each country-year a category against written definitions, so a change in category is a judgement about a defining feature.

concepts.title: Count and share
concepts.summary: A count says how many; a share divides it by a total. A count can rise while a share falls.

concepts.title: Denominator
concepts.summary: What a percentage is a percentage of; turnout here is a share of registered voters, not of adults.

concepts.title: Gap in a series
concepts.summary: A year or country with no row, which says nothing by itself about what happened.

concepts.title: Anomaly
concepts.summary: A value, or a run of identical values, that is unlikely enough to need checking before it is used.

misconceptions: Reading a category change as a verdict on a government. It is experts' coding against the definitions in 2K to 2N, and a one-step change means a defining feature was judged to have changed.
Treating high turnout as a sign of democracy. Turnout is a share of registered voters (3B). Iran's 91.7 in 1963 falls in a year the regime data code as closed autocracy.
Reading a count as a share. Closed autocracies held about 2.02 billion people in 1990 and 2.22 billion in 2022, yet their share fell from 38.1% to 27.7%, because the total grew.
Reading a missing row as 'no regime'. Germany has no rows from 1945 to 1990 and the pack does not say why.
sequence: Always read the definition first: 2K to 2N for regimes, 3B for turnout, 3C for women in parliament.
Read a country as runs of one category (Germany, Japan, Brazil, Egypt); questions on first year and length of a run.
Gaps and anomalies: Germany's missing years; the United States turnout values 70.75 three times in a row.
Counts and shares: compute the share of people in democracies in 1990 and 2022 and compare with Wikipedia's claim (3D).
What turnout can show: Australia and Sweden against Iran and Egypt, and what the denominator hides.
A third series, women in the lower chamber, as a measure that is not about regimes: Saudi Arabia (19.9) above India (13.8) in 2025; the PR claim (8Y) and why two countries cannot test it.
Why indices disagree (3E, 3F, 3G): minimalist against maximalist definitions.
examples: First year coded liberal democracy: Sweden 1922, France 1947, Japan 1952, United States 1969, Germany 1991.

lessons.title: Montesquieu and the separation of powers
lessons.objective: Use Montesquieu's definitions to say which power an act belongs to, use his and Madison's arguments to test a described arrangement, and set Bagehot's opposite view beside them.

concepts.title: Legislative, executive and judiciary power
concepts.summary: Montesquieu's three: making and repealing laws; making peace or war, embassies and security; punishing crimes and settling disputes between individuals.

concepts.title: Separation of powers
concepts.summary: The principle that these powers be held by different persons or bodies.

concepts.title: Checks and balances
concepts.summary: Constitutional means by which each branch can limit the others, such as a veto.

concepts.title: Fusion of powers
concepts.summary: A system in which executive and legislature are joined, as in the Westminster parliamentary systems.

concepts.title: Union of the three powers
concepts.summary: Montesquieu's example is the Sultan in Turkey, where all three are united in one person.

misconceptions: Thinking separation means the branches never touch. Madison says each department needs the means and motives to resist the others (4H), and Wikipedia gives the presidential veto as a legislative power in the hands of the executive (4K).
Reading Montesquieu's 'executive' as only carrying out laws. In his definition it includes making peace or war, sending and receiving embassies, public security and defence against invasion (4A).

Assuming everyone has thought separation wise. Bagehot praised the fusion of executive and legislature (4J), Paine denied that liberty rests on the form of government (4M), and Wikipedia says Hobbes opposed separation (4P).
Reading checks as a pure good. Wikipedia notes that vetoes can produce gridlock when veto players disagree (4L).
sequence: Begin with Montesquieu's three definitions (4A); the learner places six acts under the three.
Read why the judiciary must stand apart (4B) and why one holder of all three means the end of everything (4C), with his contrast of moderate European kingdoms and Turkey (4D).
Montesquieu on appointment: if the legislature appoints the others, the power to appoint carries the power to revoke (4Q).
Madison's step beyond the lines on paper: each department needs the means and the motive (4H), because 'if men were angels' no government would be needed (4I).
The executive's share in lawmaking by rejecting (4G) and the presidential veto as a legislative power (4K); the cost in gridlock (4L).
Set the critics beside the theory: Bagehot's fusion (4J), Paine (4M); Hobbes's opposition (4P).
Where separation is the norm, and where fusion is (4N); carry the question to lesson 6.
examples: Invented acts to place: an assembly raises the tax on salt (legislative); a ministry sends an envoy to settle a border (executive); a court fines a merchant for fraud (judiciary); a tribunal settles a dispute over a boundary stone between neighbours (judiciary); the government sends troops to the frontier against invasion (executive); parliament repeals an old weights law (legislative).
A legislature that also sits as the highest court: Montesquieu says the judge would then be the legislator (4B).
A legislature that appoints the judges and may remove them at will: under 4Q the power to appoint carries the power to revoke.

lessons.title: Reading a constitution
lessons.objective: From the text of the United States Constitution (1787) and the Australian Constitution (1900 as enacted), say which body holds a named power, whether another body must agree, and what checks it.

concepts.title: Vested power
concepts.summary: The word both texts use to say where a power rests: legislative power 'vested in' Congress, executive power 'vested in' a President or the Queen.

concepts.title: Advice and consent
concepts.summary: The Senate's part in treaties and appointments in the American text: the President acts with its agreement.

concepts.title: Appropriation
concepts.summary: A law that authorises money to be drawn from the treasury; both texts say no money may be drawn without one.

concepts.title: Impeachment
concepts.summary: Removal from office on conviction of treason, bribery or other high crimes and misdemeanors; the House accuses and the Senate tries.

concepts.title: Text and practice
concepts.summary: A constitution's words and the way it is worked can differ; the Australian text never mentions a Prime Minister or Cabinet.

misconceptions: Assuming the text says what practice does. The Australian text vests executive power in the Queen, exercised by the Governor-General (5Q), and does not contain the words Prime Minister or Cabinet (checked by search of the pack file); Wikipedia says the appointment of a prime minister is technically a prerogative of the head of state (5Y).
Counting a power as one body's when the text splits it. Treaties need two thirds of the Senators present, and Supreme Court judges are appointed with the Senate's advice and consent (5I).
Thinking 'executive' means only the President. In the Australian text ministers hold office at the Governor-General's pleasure and must sit in Parliament within three months (5R, 5S).

Treating the pack's American text as the present one. It is the 1787 text without Amendments XI to XXVII; for example it has Senators chosen by state legislatures, and Wikipedia's federalism article says the US did elect its upper house indirectly before 1913 (see lesson 12).
sequence: Where does legislative power sit? Compare 5A (Congress) with 5P (the Queen, a Senate and a House of Representatives).
Executive power: 5G and 5Q; then ministers (5R, 5S) the Governor-General's discretion over assent to a bill (5X) and the text/practice gap (5Y).
Judicial power: 5M, 5N and 5T, 5U; note that nothing in the pack says courts may strike down laws (see lesson 7).
Shared powers: the path of a bill and the veto (5B, 5C), revenue bills (5Z, 5W), treaties and appointments (5I). The learner orders the path of a vetoed bill.
The purse: taxes (5D), money from the treasury only by law (5F, 5V), war and armies (5E). Compare the two texts side by side.
Removal: impeachment (5J, 5K, 5L) and judges (5U).
A seat-allocation rule written into a constitution is in lesson 9; here the learner assigns powers and names checks.
examples: Assign seven US powers: declare war (Congress, 5E); grant pardons for offences against the United States (President, 5H); try an impeachment (the Senate, so Congress, 5K); decide a case arising under the Constitution (the courts, 5N); make a treaty (President and Senate, 5I); appoint a Supreme Court judge (President and Senate, 5I); command the army and navy (President, 5H).

The path of a vetoed bill: both houses pass it; it goes to the President; he returns it with his objections to the house where it began; that house repasses it by two thirds; the other house also repasses it by two thirds and it becomes law (5B, 5C).

Two sentences on money: 'No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law' (5F) and 'No money shall be drawn from the Treasury of the Commonwealth except under appropriation made by law' (5V).

lessons.title: Parliamentary, presidential and mixed systems
lessons.objective: Classify a country's system as parliamentary, presidential or semi-presidential from how its head of government is chosen and removed, and say what each arrangement does to the separation Montesquieu described.

concepts.title: Confidence
concepts.summary: The support of a majority of parliament on which a parliamentary head of government depends; losing a vote of no confidence ends it.

concepts.title: Presidential system
concepts.summary: A head of government elected separately from the legislature and not removable by it except in extraordinary cases.

concepts.title: Semi-presidential system
concepts.summary: A president alongside a prime minister and cabinet who answer to the legislature.

concepts.title: Cohabitation
concepts.summary: In a semi-presidential system, a president and prime minister from different parties.

concepts.title: Dualism
concepts.summary: A rule that members of parliament resign their seats on becoming ministers, as in the Netherlands, Slovakia and Sweden.

misconceptions: Going by the title. Dictators and leaders of one-party states often carry the title of president (6C), and Iran has an elected president under a Supreme Leader described as the absolute power (6P).
Thinking a president named by someone else makes a system presidential. In Germany the president nominates a candidate and the Bundestag votes on them, which is parliamentary (6I).

Treating 'semi-presidential' as one pattern. In the premier-presidential subtype only parliament can remove the cabinet; in the president-parliamentary subtype the president can also dismiss it (6E, 6F).

Supposing a parliamentary system has no separation at all. Westminster systems fuse executive and legislature (6G), but dualist systems such as Sweden and the Netherlands bar overlap (6H), and Australia is described as semi-parliamentary (6Q).
sequence: Two questions: how is the head of government chosen, and who can remove them?
Parliamentary (6A): confidence; Westminster monism (6G); dualism (6H); Germany's procedure (6I).
Presidential (6B): fixed term, removal only in extraordinary cases; the title trap (6C); Iran (6P).
Semi-presidential (6D) and its two subtypes (6E, 6F); cohabitation (6N); the accountability problem (6O).
Back to the texts: ministers in Australia must sit in Parliament (5S), US officeholders may not sit in Congress (6R); apply Montesquieu's test (4E, 4O) and Bagehot's reply (4J).
Arguments for and against: Wilson's single executive (6K) and the gridlock charge (6L).
Classify six invented descriptions.
examples: Invented descriptions: a head of government who must resign if the assembly passes a no-confidence motion (parliamentary); a head of government elected for a fixed term whom the assembly cannot dismiss except for a crime (presidential); a directly elected president who appoints a prime minister whose cabinet the assembly can force out (semi-presidential).
A one-party state whose leader, called president, is chosen by the party congress and cannot be removed by any assembly vote: the title is not the test (6C).

lessons.title: What courts can and cannot do
lessons.objective: Judge what a court can do about an act of the legislature or the executive in a described case, using Hamilton's argument and the three approaches to review.

concepts.title: Judicial review
concepts.summary: A court's assessment of whether an action of the executive or, in some systems, a statute is lawful or constitutional.

concepts.title: Declaration of incompatibility
concepts.summary: In the UK, a court's finding that an Act conflicts with the Human Rights Act's rights; it does not disapply the Act and asks Parliament to act.

concepts.title: Constitutional court
concepts.summary: A court whose job is to review laws against the constitution, as in Austria and Germany.

concepts.title: Judicial independence
concepts.summary: Tenure during good behaviour and pay that cannot be reduced, so that judges can resist the other branches.

concepts.title: Review not appeal
concepts.summary: In review of an official decision the court asks whether it was lawful; it does not usually retake the decision.

misconceptions: Thinking the judiciary is the strongest branch because it can void laws. Hamilton calls it the weakest: it controls neither sword nor purse and depends on the executive for the efficacy of its judgments (7A).
Thinking review makes courts superior to legislatures. Hamilton answers that the power of the people is superior to both (7D).
Thinking every democracy lets courts strike down statutes. The UK and the Netherlands do not (7J, 7L); UK courts may issue declarations of incompatibility only (7K).
Confusing review of an official decision with an appeal (7Q).

Thinking the American text gives the power. Wikipedia says the US Constitution as drafted did not codify it and that the Supreme Court took the step in Marbury v. Madison (7P); Hamilton argued for it in Federalist 78 (dated 28 May 1788 in the file).
sequence: Montesquieu's judges as 'the mouth that pronounces the words of the law' (4F) and Hamilton's 'neither force nor will, but merely judgment' (7A).
Why tenure matters (7F), and the texts (5M, 5T, 5U).

The argument for review in order: limits need courts (7B); an act contrary to its commission is void (7C); the Constitution is fundamental law (7G); the people are superior to both (7D); the objection of will against judgment (7E).

The three approaches: none (UK, Netherlands: 7J, 7L), general courts (Australia, Canada, US, India: 7M, 7N), specialised court (Czechoslovakia, Austria: 7O; Germany: 7R). The learner sorts six countries.
The UK middle path (7K): a declaration, not a strike-down.
Review is not appeal (7Q) and what the pack says on the US text (7P). The plain definition of review is 7I.
What a court cannot do: enforce its own judgment (7A); the UN Charter's Article 94 in lesson 13 is the same point between states.
examples: A UK court finds an Act incompatible with Convention rights under the Human Rights Act 1998: it can issue a declaration; Parliament decides whether to change the law (7K).
An official refuses a residence permit and the applicant goes to court. The court asks whether the decision followed the law and procedure, not whether it would have decided the same (7Q).
Six countries to place: UK and Netherlands (no review of statutes), Australia and India (general courts), Austria and Germany (specialised constitutional court).

lessons.title: From votes to seats
lessons.objective: Work out how many seats each party wins from district results under first-past-the-post and from vote totals under D'Hondt and under largest remainder with the Hare quota, find the Droop quota for a single-transferable-vote district, measure the gap with the Gallagher index, and read a constitution's seat rule.

concepts.title: Plurality (first past the post)
concepts.summary: In each single-member district the candidate with the most votes wins, even without a majority.

concepts.title: D'Hondt method
concepts.summary: A highest-averages method: each party's votes are divided by 1, 2, 3 and so on, and the highest quotients, as many as there are seats, win.

concepts.title: Largest remainder method
concepts.summary: Each party's votes are divided by a quota; each party gets the whole number, and leftover seats go to the largest fractional remainders. With the Hare quota (votes divided by seats) it is Hamilton's method.

concepts.title: Droop quota
concepts.summary: Total votes divided by the number of seats plus one; more than that guarantees a seat. As a share it is 1 over k plus 1.

concepts.title: Gallagher index
concepts.summary: The square root of half the sum of the squared differences between each party's vote percent and seat percent.

misconceptions: Assuming the party with the most votes wins the most seats. Under plurality a party can win a majority of seats with a minority of votes, and sometimes the second-placed party in votes wins most seats (8C, 8E).

Treating 'proportional' as one method, or as exact. D'Hondt and the Hare largest remainder method give different seats from the same votes: Wikipedia says D'Hondt favours large parties (8AE) and that the Hare quota is unbiased between large and small (8AI); exact proportionality is never achieved except by chance (8K).
Confusing the Hare and Droop quotas. Hare is votes divided by seats; Droop is votes divided by seats plus one, the least that guarantees a seat (8AJ, 8AN).

Treating one system as plainly fairer. The pack gives arguments each way: supporters of FPTP cite majority governments (8H), supporters of PR cite fairness and coalitions that force compromise (8I); opponents say two-party plurality systems avoid the problems of coalitions, and the pack records the reply that this is not necessarily so (8J).

Reading a Gallagher index as a verdict on a country. It measures the gap between vote and seat shares in one election; the pack's real values (8AW to 8BA) show it varies with system and election, and say nothing about causes beyond the system named.
sequence: The rule and a first case: plurality in one district, the Tennessee capital vote with first preferences of 42, 26, 17 and 15 percent (8A, 8B).
District by district in an invented country: five districts, three parties. The learner finds each winner and the seat totals, and compares seat share with vote share.

Real cases: UK 2024, Reform UK 14.3% of votes and 5 seats, Liberal Democrats 12.2% and 72 seats (8C), and why concentrated support wins seats (8AA); UK 2015 votes per seat (8D); Canada's two provinces (8F); wasted votes (8G); just over a quarter of the vote can win a majority (8E).

D'Hondt: the definition (8AB), the procedure (8AC, 8AD), the pack's own example without its table (8AG), its history (8AF) and its bias towards large parties (8AE). The learner allocates 8 seats from the invented country's vote totals.

Largest remainder with the Hare quota: the method (8AH), the quota (8AJ) and the steps (8AK), where it is used (8AL), and Hare against Droop (8AI, 8AS, 8AT). The learner allocates the same 8 seats and sees the two methods differ.

The Gallagher index: its definition (8AU, 8AV; the PR article states it too, 8L), computed for the three results, and real values: Canada 2015 under plurality 12.02, Queensland 2012 31.16, Sweden 2022 0.64, Ireland 2020 1.96 (8AW, 8AX, 8AY, 8AZ) and the target of 5 or less (8M).

STV and the Droop quota: definition (8AM), formula (8AN, 8AO), the pack's worked count (8AP, 8AQ), the Hare quota in a count (8AR), the three-seat case (8N), Malta and New South Wales (8O, 8P), and thresholds (8Q, 8R).
A constitution can write the seat rule itself: Australia's section 24 and the minimum of five (8U, 8V, 8W, 8X). The learner computes a House from invented populations.
Arguments for and against, without a verdict: 8H, 8I, 8J, and Mill's case for proportional representation (8S, 8T).
examples: Invented country, five districts of 10,000 votes, 50,000 in all: X wins three districts and has 33.6% of votes; Y wins two and has 56.4%; Z wins none with 10.0%. Seat shares 60, 40, 0.

Eight seats from the same totals (X 16,800, Y 28,200, Z 5,000). D'Hondt quotients in order: Y 28,200; X 16,800; Y 14,100; Y 9,400; X 8,400; Y 7,050; Y 5,640; X 5,600. The next, Z's 5,000, misses. Result X 3, Y 5, Z 0. Largest remainder with the Hare quota 50,000 / 8 = 6,250: X 2.69, Y 4.51, Z 0.80; wholes 2, 4, 0; the two leftover seats go to Z (.80) and X (.69). Result X 3, Y 4, Z 1.
Gallagher index of the three results against vote shares 33.6, 56.4 and 10.0: plurality 23.09, D'Hondt 8.73, largest remainder with Hare 5.59.
Droop quota as a share, 1 over k plus 1: 25 percent for 3 seats, 16.7 percent for 5 (the pack gives Malta's as 16.6), 4.5 percent (1/22) for 21, 10 percent for 9.

Australia's section 24 with invented populations (not Australia's): 36 senators, so the quota is the Commonwealth population divided by 72. With a population of 3,600,000 the quota is 50,000. States of 1,080,000, 980,000, 620,000, 480,000, 300,000 and 140,000 get 22, 20, 12, 10, 6 and 5 members; the last because of the minimum of five. The House has 75 members, not 72.

lessons.title: Factions, parties and interest groups
lessons.objective: Read Madison's argument in Federalist 10 as a chain of claims and apply it to a case, and tell a party, an interest group and a faction inside a party apart by what each is for.

concepts.title: Faction (Madison)
concepts.summary: A number of citizens, a majority or a minority, united by a common passion or interest against others' rights or the community's interests.

concepts.title: Republic (Madison)
concepts.summary: A government in which a small number of elected citizens act for the rest, which can cover a larger area than a pure democracy.

concepts.title: Political party
concepts.summary: An organisation that coordinates candidates to compete in elections and take part in governing.

concepts.title: Interest or advocacy group
concepts.summary: An organisation that seeks to influence public opinion and policy without, as a rule, running candidates.

concepts.title: Free rider problem
concepts.summary: People gain from a group's success without joining or paying, which weakens the group.

misconceptions: Reading 'faction' as a wing of a party. In Madison it means any group, majority or minority, acting against others' rights or the community's interests (9A); in the Wikipedia party article a political faction is a subgroup within a party (9K).
Thinking Madison wants to remove faction. He says its causes cannot be removed without destroying liberty or making everyone think alike, so he looks to controlling its effects (9B, 9C, 9E).
Using 'republic' as a synonym for 'democracy'. Madison defines a republic by representation and a democracy as a society that assembles and governs in person (9G, 9S).
Assuming interest groups run candidates, or that only democracies have parties. A party focuses on electing candidates (9K), parties also exist in autocracies, and some autocracies ban them (9O, 2Q).
sequence: Madison's problem and definition (9A); the two methods of cure (9B); why the first is worse than the disease (9C).
Where faction comes from: the most common source is unequal property (9D), so the cure is control of effects (9E).
A minority faction is checked by the vote; a majority faction is not (9F); why a pure democracy has no cure (9S).
The republic as the answer (9G, 9I) and the large republic (9H).
Parties: definition (9J) and how they differ from groups, factions and parliamentary groups (9K).
Interest groups: definition (9L), the free-rider problem (9M), pluralism (9N).
Party systems: one-party and bans (9O, 9R), Duverger's law and its debate (9P), multi-party (9Q); link back to lesson 8.
examples: Invented organisations to classify: an organisation that nominates candidates under one label and tries to form a government (party); a trade association that lobbies for lower import duties and endorses no candidate (interest group); a group of legislators inside a party who press its leaders to adopt a stricter budget (faction within a party).
A town of 400 settles every question at a meeting where each adult votes, and a majority shares an interest in taxing a minority. Under 9S there is nothing to check it.

lessons.title: From public opinion to policy and budget
lessons.objective: Place a described event at its stage in the policy cycle and say who acts there, read a simple government budget as receipts, spending and balance, and say what the pack does and does not tell us about public opinion.

concepts.title: Agenda setting
concepts.summary: The stage at which problems that need government attention are identified and ranked.

concepts.title: Policy cycle
concepts.summary: A sequence of stages: agenda setting, policy formulation, legitimation, implementation and evaluation.

concepts.title: Legitimation
concepts.summary: The gathering of approval for a policy from an executive, a legislature or the public, through consultation or referendum.

concepts.title: Government budget
concepts.summary: A projection of revenue and spending for a period; it does not itself appropriate funds.

concepts.title: Deficit
concepts.summary: Spending above receipts, usually financed by borrowing, which builds up as debt.

concepts.title: Bureaucracy
concepts.summary: The system in which civil servants, not elected officials, put laws and regulations into effect.

misconceptions: Treating the cycle as strictly one-way. The stages vary by author, a non-linear framework exists, and evaluation can send an issue back to the agenda (10H, 10N).
Taking a poll as a reading of opinion that already exists. People often give pseudo-opinions to please the questioner (10D) and framing shapes what they think (10C).
Thinking passing a law finishes a policy. The pack describes an implementation gap between goals on paper and practice (10M), and says a budget does not itself appropriate funds (10P).
Confusing deficit with debt. A deficit is spending above receipts in a period; accumulated borrowing creates debt (10S).
sequence: What public opinion is (10A) and how it forms: agenda setting by media (10B), framing (10C), pseudo-opinions (10D). The pack's one line on polls (10F); the pack has no poll data and no method.
The policy cycle as a whole (10G, 10H), each stage in turn: agenda setting (10I), formulation (10J), legitimation (10K), implementation (10L), evaluation (10N). The learner orders an invented case.
Opinion and policy cause each other (10E, 10E2).
Where the legislature and the money come in: appropriation by law in both constitutional texts (5F, 5V, 5Z, 5W); a budget is not itself an appropriation (10P), and it is defined in 10O.
Reading a budget: receipts (10V, 10W, 10Q), spending, and the balance (10R, 10S, 10T). The learner works out the balance of an invented budget.
A budget is also political (10U); the history of budgets auditable by parliament (10X).
Who carries it out: bureaucracy, its two dilemmas (10Y), Weber's view (10Z) and the implementation gap (10M).
examples: Invented flood case in order: residents and newspapers press the council to treat flooding as a problem (agenda setting); officials draft a plan with options and costs (formulation); the council votes to approve the plan and funds (legitimation); a new agency builds the barriers (implementation); auditors measure whether flooding has fallen (evaluation).

Invented budget (millions): receipts 350 income tax, 220 sales tax, 60 fees and charges, 20 grants, total 650; spending 210 health, 140 education, 230 pensions, 90 defence, total 670; a deficit of 20.

lessons.title: Rights and the majority
lessons.objective: Apply Mill's principle on liberty to a described law and say whether it passes his test, use Tocqueville to name a way a majority can limit liberty without any law, and read who a rights clause restrains.

concepts.title: Mill's principle
concepts.summary: Power may rightfully be used against a member of a community, against his will, only to prevent harm to others; his own good is not enough.

concepts.title: Tyranny of the majority
concepts.summary: Oppression of a minority or of individuals by a ruling majority; Mill and Tocqueville use the phrase and differ in emphasis.

concepts.title: Social tyranny
concepts.summary: Pressure by prevailing opinion and feeling, without legal penalties, that Mill says can be more formidable than political oppression.

concepts.title: Civil liberties
concepts.summary: Fundamental rights and freedoms that governments pledge not to restrict without due process of law.

concepts.title: State of emergency
concepts.summary: A power in many constitutions to suspend some rights in exceptional circumstances, which the pack says has been abused.

misconceptions: Taking Mill to say the state may never limit conduct. His principle allows compulsion to prevent harm to others (11A) and rules out a person's own good as a warrant (11B).
Believing majority rule guarantees liberty. Mill and Tocqueville each argue otherwise (11D, 11G, 11H), and Wikipedia says that without legal protections political minorities can be oppressed (11Q).

Thinking tyranny of the majority is always done by law. Mill says society can practise a tyranny more formidable than many political ones by means other than civil penalties (11E, 11F); Tocqueville says the majority acts on the will as well as the actions (11I), though he says abuses are not frequent (11J).
Reading a bill of rights as protecting people from one another. The first proposed article says 'Congress shall make no law' (11K): it restrains the lawmaker.

Treating rights as absolute in emergencies. The pack says suspension in war and emergency is debated (11O) and can be abused (11P); the UDHR (paraphrase only) allows limits fixed by law for others' rights and a democratic society's needs.
sequence: Mill's setting: the old fear of the magistrate and the newer fear of society itself (11D, 11E, 11F).
The principle (11A), what it excludes (11B) and what it leaves to the individual (11C). The learner sorts six invented laws.
Tocqueville: a people has no right to do whatever it pleases (11G); a majority is like a monarch that can wrong its adversaries (11H).
How the majority limits thought (11I), and his hedge (11J). Pair Mill and Tocqueville.
What a rights text does: who is restrained by 11K, 11L and 11M; the distinction between civil liberties and other rights (11N).
Emergencies (11O, 11P) and the UDHR's Article 29 (11W, paraphrase only).
End on what the principle does not settle: where harm begins. Note that the pack also describes a libertarian lineage for Mill's view in the civil liberties article.
examples: Invented laws to test: a town fines residents who play loud music at 3 a.m. (allowed: harm to neighbours); a law forbids adults to eat food the council thinks unhealthy though it harms no one else (not allowed: own good); a rule forbids adults to read a newspaper the council thinks foolish (not allowed); a law requires drivers to stop at red lights (allowed); a law makes it an offence to leave a gate open that lets cattle onto a neighbour's crops (allowed); a law punishes a habit the majority finds distasteful though it affects no one else (not allowed).
'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion' restrains Congress, the maker of laws, and not private groups.

lessons.title: Federal and unitary states
lessons.objective: Say from a description or constitutional text whether a state is federal or unitary, which level holds a power, who can change the division, and whether a referendum passes under a double-majority rule.

concepts.title: Federal state
concepts.summary: A state that divides governing powers between a central government and regional governments, in a constitution.

concepts.title: Unitary state
concepts.summary: A state in which the central government is the supreme authority; regions exercise only powers it chooses to delegate.

concepts.title: Devolution
concepts.summary: Delegation of powers by a central government to regions, which the central government can alter.

concepts.title: Residual powers
concepts.summary: The powers not listed in the constitution; they go to the states in Germany and the United States, to the centre in Canada and India.

concepts.title: Double majority
concepts.summary: A rule that an amendment needs a majority of voters nationally and a majority in a majority of the states.

misconceptions: Calling devolution federalism. In the UK, devolved powers are delegated and Parliament can change them (12I, 12C); in a federation the regions' powers are in the constitution and the centre cannot change them alone (12D).

Thinking every federation leaves unlisted powers with the states. Germany and the United States do; Canada and India do not (12G); Australia lists federal powers and leaves the rest to the States (12H, 12K).
Thinking a national majority is enough to amend. In Australia and Switzerland a proposal also needs majorities in a majority of the states or cantons (12J, 12Q).

lessons.title: States among states
lessons.objective: Apply Hobbes's argument to the relations between states, say what the Security Council can and cannot do, and judge whether a described resolution would pass.

concepts.title: Sovereignty
concepts.summary: In E-IR's words, a state's claim to the exclusive right to govern its territory and to act toward other states as it sees fit.

concepts.title: International anarchy
concepts.summary: A system in which power is decentralised and no shared institutions have the right to enforce common rules; not chaos.

concepts.title: Intergovernmental organisation
concepts.summary: An organisation of states whose power rests with the member governments, not with the organisation.

concepts.title: Veto
concepts.summary: A negative vote by one of the five permanent members, which blocks a draft resolution however many other votes it has.

concepts.title: Realism and liberalism
concepts.summary: Two theories: realists see an anarchic system in which states rely on themselves; liberals see room for cooperation and a democratic peace.

misconceptions: Thinking the UN is a world government. E-IR says its power rests with member governments, it has no army of its own, and punishment needs the Security Council's accord and states willing to act (13M, 13Q, 13R).
Reading international anarchy as chaos. It means no shared institution has the right to enforce common rules (13D).

Thinking a veto can stop any discussion. Procedural matters and discussion cannot be vetoed (13U); abstention is not usually regarded as a veto (13V); and the veto does not carry into the General Assembly, whose votes are non-binding (13S2).
Thinking international law is not law because there is no world government. E-IR names its sources (treaties, custom, general principles) and says states are bound by what they consent to (13K, 13L).
sequence: Hobbes on sovereigns who face one another like gladiators (13A); what 'sovereign' means (13B) and how many there are (13C).
Anarchy among states (13D) and the realist reading of Hobbes (13E, 13F); the liberal reply, Kant and the democratic peace (13G, 13H); organisations in each view (13I, 13J).
Law without a world government: 13K and the sources in 13L.
International organisations: power rests with states (13M); UN membership (13N); General Assembly one state one vote (13O); Security Council (13P, 13S).

The voting rule: nine votes, a permanent member's negative vote blocks (13T), procedural matters and discussion cannot be vetoed (13U), abstention (13V), the veto record (13W). The learner judges four invented votes.

What the Council can do and who pays: binding under Chapter VII (13X); no army (13Q); punishment needs accord and states (13R); the ICJ's judgments are enforced only through the Security Council (13UN4, paraphrase only).
Return to Hobbes: the UN is not a sovereign over states (13UN1, 13UN2, paraphrase only).
examples: Four invented votes: 13 for, 1 permanent member against, 1 abstaining (blocked); 9 for including all five permanent members and 6 against, none permanent (passes); 8 for and 7 abstaining (fails, under nine); a procedural vote with 10 for and 5 against including permanent members (passes, since procedural matters need nine votes and cannot be vetoed).
Veto counts to the end of 2024: Russia and the Soviet Union about 120, the United States 89, the United Kingdom 29, France and China 16 each (13W).
